title: Brythonic Kingdoms
capsule: The Brythons (Celtic Britons) were the Celtic-speaking inhabitants of Great Britain, attested in Greco-Roman sources from the Iron Age and speakers of Common Brittonic, the ancestor of Welsh, Cornish, and Breton. Roman conquest from 43 CE progressively incorporated southern Britain; following the Roman withdrawal in the early 5th century, the remaining Brythonic kingdoms — Strathclyde, Rheged, Gwynedd, Dumnonia, and others — resisted Anglo-Saxon expansion across lowland Britain over successive centuries. By 1066 Brythonic political identity survived only in Wales and Cornwall on the island, while a diaspora community had established Brittany across the Channel; the last independent Welsh princeship fell to Edward I of England in 1283.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Brythons are not a single bounded polity; the dataset geometry likely represents their collective presence across Britain as reconstructed from archaeological and linguistic evidence. Pre-Roman extents are broadly estimated; Roman-period territories are better documented, and post-Roman Brythonic kingdoms are reconstructed from early medieval Welsh chronicles and genealogical texts with significant uncertainty about boundaries.
